outcome: The Mixed Methods Workbench is finished to 1.0 as a general tool in Brian's broader vision, not for one use case: on two rights-clear interview corpora a person can open a study page, follow every qualitative claim to its passage, see a quantitative strand measured and checked against the authors' own coding, read a joint display with bounded meta-inferences and a gated causal check, review and export everything with full traces, and read on a benchmark page what works, what fails and what it cost. The public PsychosisBank review stays served from committed files.

entries.criterion: I can open the public review and see, for each finding, what backs it and that no causal conclusion is published yet
demonstration: Open https://psychosisbank-review.brianmills2718.workers.dev/
Scroll to the 'Independent challenge' section and read each finding's card
Click a cited excerpt's source link
entries.expected: Each finding shows its verdict, the source excerpts behind it and the remaining source gap; the page says the causal conclusion is withheld pending researcher review; the source link opens the original public document.
entries.failure_example: Finding 3's quote about 'this level' without its antecedent: a broken page shows the quote alone, with no note that the TalkBank policy names it 'Controlled access'.

representation.note: The router picked a table for one row per finding; the existing page shows the same fields as one card per finding, which reads the same way on a phone. Kept, not rebuilt.

entries.criterion: I can see which method steps the crosswalk found shared across methods, and why
demonstration: Open the crosswalk page (planned: a table rendered from docs/research/method_decomposition/phase5/adjudication.yaml; until then the file on GitHub)
Read the table of groups, one row per group of steps from two or more methods
Open one row's justification
entries.expected: 36 rows; each says same capability, shared shell or different capability with a one-line reason; today none says same capability.
entries.failure_example: A row with members from one method only, or a verdict with no reason, means the generator or the check is broken.

entries.criterion: I can open the study page for a general example corpus and follow each qualitative claim back to the interview passage it rests on, and see the corpus is frozen with its licence
demonstration: Open proposals/open-science-study/index.html (committed; served locally with `make study-page`)
Read the corpus panel: 26 interviews, licence CC BY-SA 4.0, each file's hash status
Click a category, then one of its supporting passages
Read the passage in its interview, with its speaker and the author's own codes for that span
entries.expected: Every interview shows 'hash matches Zenodo' in blue; each of QC's 8 categories and 6 propositions lists its passages; each passage opens at the right place in the right interview; the quantitative and integration strands say 'not built yet' in grey.
entries.failure_example: A passage whose offsets do not match the frozen text: a broken page shows the wrong words silently; a working page lists it under 'offset mismatches' in orange with both texts.

entries.criterion: I can see one category measured across every interview, and how well that measure agrees with the author's own coding on interviews it was not tuned on
demonstration: Open the study page's Measurement tab
Read the instrument: the rule and its included and excluded examples
Read the per-interview measure and the agreement figure with its interval
Click a disagreement and read the passage, the model's quoted reason and the author's code
entries.expected: Agreement is shown with a bootstrap interval by interview and the count of held-out interviews; every disagreement is listed and opens its passage and its model trace.
entries.failure_example: Agreement computed on the same interviews used to tune the rule: the page must say 'held out: 0' and refuse to show a figure.

entries.criterion: I can compare each qualitative proposition with the measured numbers and read whether they agree, and what may be concluded from both together
demonstration: Open the Joint display tab
Read one row per proposition: the claim, the measured distribution, the verdict
Open a row's meta-inference and its challenger's critique
entries.expected: Each row shows a verdict word (converges, complements, diverges, silent) with the passages and numbers it rests on; every meta-inference says 'pending review' until reviewed.
entries.failure_example: A meta-inference that claims more than either strand supports (for example a population rate from 26 interviews): the challenger flags it in orange and it is not marked accepted.

entries.criterion: I can see a causal check on one proposition kept apart from how common it is, and that no causal conclusion shows unless the gate allows it
demonstration: Open the Causal tab
Read the hypothesis, each evidence test and its verdict
Read the publication gate line
entries.expected: Process Tracing's within-case verdicts are shown in their own panel, never merged with the prevalence; the conclusion shows only when the gate says publishable, else 'withheld' and why.
entries.failure_example: A Process Tracing export whose gate is not publishable: a broken page still shows the causal conclusion.

entries.criterion: I can accept, reject or annotate each meta-inference, see it saved, and download one bundle with every trace
demonstration: Run `make study-workbench` and open the local address it prints
Accept one meta-inference and reject another with a note
Reload the page
Click 'Download bundle' and open its manifest
entries.expected: Decisions survive the reload and appear in the review log; the bundle's manifest lists every file with its hash, including each run's trace and the reporting checklist.
entries.failure_example: A decision that vanishes on reload, or a bundle file whose hash differs from its manifest line.

entries.criterion: I can see on two different corpora what the workbench gets right, what it gets wrong, which planted failures it catches, and what each run cost
demonstration: Open the benchmark page
Read one row per corpus and strand: agreement with the authors' coding
Read the planted-failure table
Read cost and time per run with its basis
entries.expected: Both corpora appear; every planted failure is listed as caught (blue) or missed (orange); costs cite their llm-cost measurement.
entries.failure_example: A planted altered quote that the checks pass: the row reads 'missed' in orange, not hidden.

entries.criterion: I can see which methods the finished workbench actually runs and which it does not
demonstration: Open the method-profile page
Filter to 'runs in 1.0'
Read the reason beside an unsupported method
entries.expected: Every method profile carries runs / does not run, the latter with a one-line reason; the release notes list both lists.
entries.failure_example: A method marked as run with no slice or test behind it.

entries.criterion: I can point the workbench at a corpus it has never seen and get the same study page, without anyone changing its code
demonstration: Open the benchmark page's 'corpora' list and the second corpus's study page
Open the second corpus's study definition file (the only file added for it)
Read the commit that added the corpus: it changes no file under src/
entries.expected: The second corpus's study page has the same panels as the first; it was added by one study definition file plus frozen data; the page states which corpus fields were required and which were optional.
entries.failure_example: A corpus name, file layout or code list written into the workbench's code: the commit adding the second corpus touches src/, and the benchmark page shows that commit in orange.

mappings.outcome_reason: The outcome says 'finished to 1.0' and enumerates every deliverable strand, keeping the requirement in full.

mappings.coverage_reason: A10 requires the workbench to accept a never-seen corpus with no code changes — it fails if the tool is hard-coded to one use case; A8 requires correct results on two distinct corpora, failing if only one is wired in.
